title: Come Worship, and Don't Harden Your Heart
overview: This psalm invites people to sing and bow before the LORD as Creator and Shepherd, then turns to a sober warning drawn from Israel's grumbling in the wilderness.

parts.label: A call to joyful worship (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The singer invites everyone to praise God together, out loud and gladly, with thanks and music. Calling God the "Rock" pictures him as solid ground and a safe place, the one who rescues.

parts.label: King over all creation (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: In a world where every nation had its own gods, the psalm claims the LORD is the great King above them all. From the deepest places to the mountain tops, sea and land belong to him because he made them.

parts.label: Kneeling before the Shepherd (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: The mood shifts from shouting to bowing low, a posture of respect before the one who made his people. The image then turns tender: they are his flock, fed and cared for like sheep.

parts.label: A warning from the wilderness (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: Suddenly God speaks, urging the people not to be stubborn like their ancestors at Massah and Meribah, names meaning "testing" and "quarreling." There, after escaping Egypt, the people demanded water and doubted God was with them, even though they had already seen him act for them.

parts.label: Forty years and a lost rest (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: That generation wandered forty years and died before entering the promised land, which is the "rest" meant here: a settled home after the journey. The psalm ends on this hard note, and Christians later read "rest" more widely, as the letter to the Hebrews does when it quotes these verses.

disagreement: Christians differ on what the promised "rest" ultimately points to: a present peace with God, a future home after death, or both together.
think: When have you seen something clearly in a good season, then found it hard to trust or remember once things got difficult?
